Why Study the LSERO with Bilateral Contracting

Project No. 58777

Thomas L. Darte – February 17, 2026

Background

Shortly after electric deregulation was adopted in 1999, my subcommittee of the ERCOT
Board of Directors issued reliability recommendations. At that time, there was discussion
of adopting a capacity market. My committee recommended that all Retail Electric
Providers (REPs), municipal utilities, and cooperatives be required to firm their load with
enough generation capacity to supply their peak demand plus reserves, expressed as a
percentage of peak demand.

Neither a capacity market nor our recommendations were adopted. Policymakers
assumed that competition alone would get plants built, and later the energy‑only scarcity
pricing model was adopted. Since then, very few turbine‑driven generation plants have
been added, even as renewables have expanded dramatically.

Winter Storm Uri exposed the consequences of this approach: massive overcharges,
lawsuits, bankruptcies, and securitization bonds that will burden Texans for years. Yet the
same scarcity pricing model remains in place. What public benefit does it provide other
than enabling extreme profit‑taking during crises?

The LSERO Concept and SB 3

After Uri, in September 2021, a white paper sponsored by NRG and Exelon—The Load
Serving Entity Reliability Obligation (LSERO)—was produced by E3 and Beth Garza. It
remains the foundational resource for understanding LSERO as a market design option for
ERCOT.

I supported this plan in my filing in Project 52373 (Generation Adequacy in ERCOT, 3/7/22).
LSERO closely resembles the reliability framework my subcommittee recommended
decades earlier: a reserve margin expressed as a percentage of peak load, typically around
15%.

Senate Bill 3 (2021) charged the PUC with the responsibility to “fix the grid.” It is essential
to be clear about who bears responsibility if the grid fails again—and to remember
ERCOT’s responsibility to the Commission.

PCM Chosen, Then Rejected, While Reliability Waits
 In November 2022, the PUC evaluated LSERO alongside five other market design options,
including the Performance Credit Mechanism (PCM). The PUC selected the PCM. The
Legislature rejected it in 2023. Instead, HB 1500 was adopted, along with the Texas Energy
Fund and a market modification called the DRRS.

E3’s modeling at that time determined that 5,630 MW of additional generation was needed
to meet the industry‑recognized reliability standard of 0.1 days per year Loss of Load
Expectation (LOLE).

At the April 17, 2023, PCM workshop, E3 reported that 13,000 MW of new dispatchable
capacity would be required to meet the same reliability standard, and that operating costs
would be lowered by an average of $5.9 billion per year if those plants were built. They also
stated that the model used to determine the 13,000 MW requirement could be used in
future ERCOT studies—including the Reliability Standard study scheduled for 2026.

During the 2025 legislative session, there was no discussion of a replacement market
design after PCM was rejected. HB 1500 placed an “economic optimization” modification
ahead of reliability. The obvious question is: when does reliability become important
enough to drive market design decisions?

New Studies, Explosive Load Growth, and Limited Sites

On November 10, 2025, ERCOT released a study by Aurora Energy Research concluding
that the measures in HB 1500 will not be sufficient to meet expected load growth and that
loss of load is probable within five years.

ERCOT’s revised load projections during the 2025 session estimated that 45–60 GW of new
generation will be needed within six years—an unprecedented 75% increase above the
current summer peak of 84 GW. Yet only about 30 GW of transmission‑ready sites exist
where plants can be built.

Modern Data Centers will want to be located at those 30GW transmission locations. They
have been compared to steel mills with rapid changes in load requiring more installed and
spinning reserves and fast ramp rates that can only be provided by combustion turbines
and reciprocating engines making it nearly impossible to chase scarcity price spikes and
rapid load changes at the same time. Generation plants that supply this load will need
financing through bilateral contracts with LSEs.

SB 6 adopted in 2025 discussions raised concern about data centers, but the focus was on
transmission financing and the “kill switch". But there was no sense of urgency about
modifying the present market design in the 2025 Senate Business & Commerce and House
State Affairs hearings.
 Why Study LSERO with Bilateral Contracting Now

Texas must build new dispatchable plants to maintain reliability. There is no alternative to
turbine‑driven technology for moment‑to‑moment frequency control. Renewables cannot
provide that function alone.

ERCOT must complete the Reliability Standard study in 2026. The same model used for
that study can simultaneously evaluate LSERO with Bilateral Contracting, saving critical
time. The LSERO study would simply use a competitive tool Texas already relies on—
bilateral contracts—and examine what happens when all Load Serving Entities (LSEs)
participate fairly in the cost of reliability. This is not a radical change in market philosophy;
it replaces a design flaw in the existing design.

A straightforward allocation method is available: require each LSE to supply dispatchable
generation capacity equal to the same percentage of its peak firm demand as the ERCOT
system. The allocation must be verifiable because large sums of money are involved.

If all LSEs procure their fair share of needed plants through bilateral contracts (which is not
required today), generators receive the predictable revenue they said they needed in the
2021 LSERO study. New plants get built, price spikes are no longer necessary, and the total
system cost of serving existing and new load becomes knowable.

LSE sharing is not a penalty; it is an obligation to share the cost of reliability.

The Savol Model and the Reliability Standard

The ERCOT Reliability Standard study uses the Savol model, which predicts the needed
amount of dispatchable generation capacity in incremental MW. When added to existing
dispatchable MW, the result is a total dispatchable capacity expressed as a percentage of
projected system peak firm demand.

The Savol model addresses the same complexities the PCM attempted to handle-
weather‑related scarcity, renewable penetration, storage, and demand‑side interruptible
loads. It simulates total system cost with added capacity for reliability—a realistic and
proven approach. Having a single MW capacity target simplifies everything. There is no
need to assign complicated and controversial performance values to each type of
resource as defined in the E3/Garza study in 2021. Competition will take care of it.

Competition, Not Central Planning

LSERO with Bilateral Contracting is a competitive enhancement, not regulation.

•      Generators—including new entrants—compete at wholesale to supply all LSEs.
 •     LSEs continue to compete at retail and choose their mix of power plants,
renewables, batteries, and demand‑side resources based on their unique load shapes.

•      All technologies can participate; competition determines the mix.

The reliability obligation is fairly shared by all LSEs, but competition—not regulation—
drives lower electricity costs for Texans. Enhanced wholesale competition “feeds” into
retail competition, allowing each LSE to assemble a resource mix tailored to its customers.
There is no need for a centrally planned, one‑size‑fits‑all capacity charge.



What the LSERO Study Would Deliver

A study of LSERO with Bilateral Contracting, conducted alongside the 2026 Reliability
Standard work, would:

•      Determine how much dispatchable capacity is needed to meet the ERCOT
Reliability Standard expressed in MW.

•      Allocate the cost fairly to all LSEs using bilateral contracts.

•      Estimate the savings to the public by installing new, efficient plants.

New, efficient plants should lower per‑unit costs and improve environmental performance
as older plants are displaced. That was true under regulation; it remains true under
competition. The scarcity pricing model is not delivering these savings but is stifling them
to achieve greater profits driving up cost to consumers in an odd form of regulation posing
as deregulation.

The Decision Needed from the PUC

All that is needed now is PUC approval for ERCOT to study LSERO with Bilateral
Contracting without delay, using the Framing Outline presented in this project. Approve the
study and learn from it. The results will show whether this plan should move forward or
whether a better alternative emerges.

Action must be taken before the 2027 legislative session. Senate Bill 3 (2021) grants the
PUC both the authority and the obligation to “fix the grid.” Authorizing an LSERO with
Bilateral Contracting study—using the same tools already being deployed for the Reliability
Standard—is a practical, competitive, and timely step toward fulfilling that obligation.
